October was a milestone month for our AI innovation: Following our roll out of Gemini 4 Argon — a frontier reasoning model — to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers, just two weeks later we announced Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model yet for long-horizon engineering and cybersecurity defense. Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward while strengthening our safety guardrails in tandem. Also in October, we introduced Genie 4, unveiled our smartest fitness tracker with Google Fitbit Edge, broke open a 20-year bottleneck in quantum computing, and more. Here’s your full recap: Introduced Gemini 4 Carbon and put Gemini 4 Argon to work. Following early safety testing, we rolled out Gemini 4 Argon globally for complex coding, financial analysis, and legal workflows across Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Google Cloud, Search, and the Gemini app, while also powering physical-world reasoning through Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics. Two weeks later, we announced Gemini 4 Carbon, which shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense. Just as we did with Argon, we’re taking a deliberate approach to rollout: Carbon is now in pre-release testing with the U.S. government and a subset of trusted cyber defenders via the Fairwind Program as we refine safety guardrails and expand partner testing ahead of a broader launch to developers, businesses, and consumers. Step into real-time interactive worlds with Genie 4. Genie 4 brings unprecedented realism, advanced physics, lifelike human movement, and native audio to real-time interactive simulation. You can steer scenes as they unfold using natural language. Genie 4 advances on our ability to create safe training environments for robots and AI agents as a crucial step toward AGI. Explore the demos on the Google DeepMind blog. Verify AI-generated content more easily around the world. # America’s retro pastime: Election betting

Election night in America used to be a party.

Before the advent of radio, election-enthusiasts gathered outside their local newspaper offices, where early returns that arrived by telegraph were immediately shared with the crowd.

On election night in 1892, for example, an estimated 250,000 people packed the streets outside The Pittsburg Dispatch, which used a limelight lantern to project the latest news onto a white curtain hung from the second story of a department store across the street. The Dispatch [reported](https://panewsarchive.psu.edu/lccn/sn84024546/1892-11-09/ed-1/seq-7.pdf) that at least half the crowd was armed with noisemakers:

“The deafening din of tin horns gathered volume every minute, until before 8 o’clock the streets downtown were hidden by dense masses of eager, howling participants, from whose lungs and mechanical organs rose a grand chorus of cheers and blasts of unearthly music.“ — 

In Duluth, MN, crowds waiting for results of the 1920 election were entertained by brass bands, movies, and professional singers. The News Tribune projected updates onto a bulletin board “every minute.” Thousands of Duluthians packed the sidewalks from 7 pm until early the next morning, the paper [reported](https://www.duluthnewstribune.com/community/in-1920-election-night-in-duluth-was-a-party).

“Police squads were kept busy clearing pathways on the sidewalk as the crowd excitedly discussed contents of the bulletins. Cold weather went unnoticed…Pictures of Republican candidates were greeted with cheering and yelling. Women vied with men in eagerness displayed as each bulletin was flashed to the public.“ — 

Nothing, however, could beat the spectacle of election night in New York City.
